content_list.content_text: For the price of a ticket, any moviegoer could witness sophistication and glamour in films like Grand Hotel (1932) and Trouble in Paradise (1932), or learn about the lives of great men such as Louis Pasteur and Emile Zola through biopics. With Citizen Kane (1941), audiences could step into the world of a contemporary celebrity, press baron William Randolph Hearst.

information.contentTitle: The famous final scene of Citizen Kane (1941)
information.contentText: Considered one of the most important films in history, introducing new techniques and styles, Citizen Kane rejected traditional linear, chronological narrative and told Kane's story entirely in flashbacks from different points of view, many of them belonging to Kane's aged and forgotten associates—the cinematic equivalent of the unreliable narrator in literature.

content_list.content_text: Every so often, the major studios felt ready to educate audiences about some of the darker aspects of American society. In 1931, Warner Bros. bought an autobiographical article by Robert Elliott Burns that had run in True Detective magazine and was later published as the book I Am a Fugitive from a Georgia Chain Gang.

content_list.title: Inventing modern cinema by ignoring conventions
content_list.description:
Citizen Kane, the directorial debut of Orson Welles (1915-1985), has always been considered "the greatest film of all time", which makes it hard to assess clearly. Myths have formed around it: that Welles pioneered a series of innovative filmmaking techniques, and that the film was dismissed on its release for being considered too pretentious.

Welles was not the first to use techniques such as greater depth of field, sets with visible ceilings, overlapping sound, jump cuts, "naturalistic" dialogue in which lines trample over one another, chiaroscuro lighting, or a narrative with multiple points of view - although no other filmmaker had dared to combine them with as much fervor and aesthetic creativity as he did.

When Citizen Kane opened, most critics received it enthusiastically, but its release was sabotaged. Press baron William Randolph Hearst had no trouble at all recognizing himself in the character of Charles Foster Kane. In the blink of an eye, his entire powerful public relations machine went into action against Welles's film, making sure it never got a decent release.

For such a revolutionary work, the message behind the film is surprisingly conventional: the rich are not to be envied for their wealth, because they have lost the simple pleasures of true love and happiness. Even so, it deserves its top status, first, because Welles's signature is so captivating, stamped so indelibly on every frame, and second, because today viewers can recognize much of Welles in the protagonist himself.

Citizen Kane is still a hugely important film, but amid its visual grandiloquence, its baroque showmanship and its ostentatious techniques - however fascinating they may be - we can hear, like a terrible premonition, the howl of frustration and creative blockage that the future held in store for the brilliant Welles.
content_list.credits: Original review by Phillip Kemp, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Despite doubts about the subject matter—one director dismissed it on the grounds that it was unsuitable at a time when people in general were so depressed that many were "jumping out of windows"—the studio persisted, and Burns, though technically still a fugitive from justice, was secretly hired to work on a first draft of the screenplay. The success of I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang (1932), directed by Mervyn LeRoy (1900-1987) and starring Paul Muni (1895-1967) as the fugitive James Allen, incisively exposed the cruelty of the penal system in the American South.

quote.quote: I always gagged on that silver spoon.
quote.author: Charles Foster Kane (Orson Welles)

content_list.content_text: Fritz Lang (1890-1976) delivered a powerful indictment of another sordid American secret. Fury (1936) was inspired by the true story of a double lynching in San Jose three years earlier. Spencer Tracy (1900-1967) plays Joe Wilson, a man wrongly accused of kidnapping a child. When a crazed mob sets fire to the jail, he manages to escape, but pretends to be dead so that those responsible will be charged with murder.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang (1932)
information.contentText: Thanks to the film, many prisoners serving on chain gangs filed appeals and were released in the United States.

content_list.content_text: In fact, nearly all the people who were lynched at the time were Black, a fact no studio was interested in publicizing. The singular power of Fury lies in the way viewers find themselves uncomfortably drawn to sympathize with the lynchers, who in turn become victims of an injustice.

Frank Capra (1897-1991) offered a more optimistic view of the anxieties of the common man. Historian Robert Sklar attributes the secret of Capra's success to "his ability to convince viewers that they were seeing their own strengths and weaknesses, their own dreams and values—in short, seeing themselves represented on the screen."

information.contentText: Billed as "the spectacle of the century," Grand Hotel made film history as the first film with an all-star cast, including Greta Garbo (1905-1990), John Barrymore (1882-1942), Joan Crawford (1904-1977), Wallace Beery (1885-1949), Lionel Barrymore (1878-1954), Lewis Stone (1879-1953), and Jean Hersholt (1886-1956). A huge box-office hit, Grand Hotel won the Oscar for Best Picture.

content_list.content_text: Capra's heroes may be victims of corrupt politicians and of capitalism, but they are not outsiders. Portraying the lives of the dispossessed on screen was more problematic. When Darryl Zanuck (1902-1979) acquired the rights to John Steinbeck's (1902-1968) novel The Grapes of Wrath (1939), the plight of the refugees of the Dust Bowl—a series of violent dust storms that devastated the southern United States in the 1930s—was a reality that many were unwilling to face.

John Ford's (1894-1973) sensitive screen version touched the collective conscience of 1940s moviegoers. Singer Woody Guthrie, who retold the story in song, summed up its importance: "Go see The Grapes of Wrath, pardner... you are the star of that picture. Go and see yourself and hear your own words and your own song."

information.contentTitle: The famous final scene of City Lights (1931)
information.contentText: Directed by Charlie Chaplin (1889-1977), City Lights is one of the deepest explorations of his Tramp persona, and its final scene is one of the most sublime moments in the history of the seventh art.

movies.title: Citizen Kane
movies.overview: Newspaper magnate, Charles Foster Kane is taken from his mother as a boy and made the ward of a rich industrialist. As a result, every well-meaning, tyrannical or self-destructive move he makes for the rest of his life appears in some way to be a reaction to that deeply wounding event.

movies.title: Grand Hotel
movies.overview: Guests at a posh Berlin hotel struggle through worry, scandal, and heartache.

movies.title: Trouble in Paradise
movies.overview: Thief Gaston Monescu and pickpocket Lily are partners in crime and love. Working for perfume company executive Mariette Colet, the two crooks decide to combine their criminal talents to rob their employer. Under the alias of Monsieur Laval, Gaston uses his position as Mariette's personal secretary to become closer to her. However, he takes things too far when he actually falls in love with Mariette, and has to choose between her and Lily.

movies.title: City Lights
movies.overview: In this sound-era silent film, a tramp falls in love with a beautiful blind flower seller.

movies.title: Fury
movies.overview: Joe, who owns a gas station along with his brothers and is about to marry Katherine, travels to the small town where she lives to visit her, but is wrongly mistaken for a wanted kidnapper and arrested.

movies.original_title: I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang
movies.title: I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang
movies.overview: A World War I veteran’s dreams of becoming a master architect evaporate in the cold light of economic realities. Things get even worse when he’s falsely convicted of a crime and sent to work on a chain gang.
